turns.q:
Your response was: "I mean... I looked through it. There were some parts that felt familiar, some that didn't quite. I'm not sure I'm the right person to say whether it all makes sense — it depends a lot on who would normally use this. I suppose some things stuck with me a bit more than others — there was more than one option, I think, near the middle of the screen, and I wasn't quite sure which one was the main one. Something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me. I couldn't say much more than that without thinking about it more."

We want to understand what you meant by "something about the way the options were presented felt a bit mixed up to me", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The visual contrast between the dark "Continue Shopping" button and the light "Place Order" button, which makes it unclear which action is primary.
B) The inconsistent formatting of the items in the "Order Summary" (specifically the bold price on the mouse), which made them look like selectable choices rather than a fixed receipt.
C) The grouping of the payment input fields (Card number, Date/CVV, Name), which felt structurally disjointed from the rest of the layout.
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: Probably A? I think — yes, that feels closest to what I meant. Something about the way those two buttons were shown, it wasn't obvious which one was the main action. I wasn't completely sure that was it, but that's the one that stood out to me.

turns.q: What specific visual attribute of the dark "Continue Shopping" button makes it feel more prominent than the "Place Order" action below it?
turns.a: There was — I think a 'Continue Shopping' button? It looked more prominent than the other one — 'Place Order,' I think. I wasn't sure if 'Continue Shopping' was the main action or if 'Place Order' was the one that was actually the main action. 'Continue Shopping' just seemed more... there. Like it had more weight behind it.

turns.q: If someone arrived at this layout ready to finalize a purchase, how would that heavier visual weight on the Continue Shopping button affect where they direct their attention first?
turns.a: I suppose... if someone just came to that screen not knowing what was expected of them, they'd probably look at 'Continue Shopping' first — because it looks more important? And then they'd have to re-read both options to figure out which one was actually the step they were supposed to do next. I'm not sure if that's how most people would see it. It might just be me.

turns.q: If the layout resolved that uncertainty about which button was the main action, would your concern disappear, or is there another structural issue with how those two options are grouped that would still stand out?
turns.a: I think — yes, probably? If 'Place Order' had a solid background and 'Continue Shopping' was the quieter one, that would probably clear up the confusion. Though I'm not certain that's all there is to it. Like, there might be something else I'm not thinking of. It's hard to say without seeing what that would actually look like.
